judgments.reasoning_cat1: The all-caps claims-made legend is boilerplate and internally definite, telling the reader coverage runs only to claims first made in the Policy Period or ERP and reported per the policy terms. Its only soft edge is the deferral 'PURSUANT TO THE TERMS HEREIN', which imports rather than creates ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is a declarations-page notice sitting against the operative grant in Section I and the deeming rules in V.A and VI.A, which can make a claim 'first made' in a period other than the one it was actually presented in; that is a harmonisable but not perfectly flush fit. In a two-policy dispute such a legend is usually quoted for context rather than construed.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A declarations item stating a 125% additional premium and a one-year ERP; the figures are definite and leave nothing to construe beyond the mislabelled item number. 'Annualized premium for the Policy Period' is a computable quantity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section II.C cross-refers to 'Item 5(A)' while the declarations line is rendered 'Item $6', a numbering slip that could be argued about but is plainly a scrivener's artifact. Item 5(B)'s one-year ERP matches II.C's one-year grant, so no substantive conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short attestation that the policy is not valid unless also signed by another authorized representative; the condition is mechanical and self-contained. Nothing in it carries two reasonable readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bears only on execution and is not contradicted by any operative term; the signature block on the declarations supplies the required signature. No other provision addresses validity.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard consideration/reliance preamble, definite in its terms and creating no operative obligation of its own. 'All information provided to the Insurer' is broad but its function is only to introduce the reliance concept.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels VIII.B (Representations and Severability), which incorporates the Application into the Policy, while VIII.K declares the Policy the 'entire agreement' — a mild recital-versus-operative tension. That tension, if litigated, would be fought on VIII.B and VIII.K rather than here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is the operative grant and it packs several construable phrases into one sentence: 'a Wrongful Act which takes place before or during the Policy Period', 'first made ... during the Policy Period', and the double reporting standard 'as soon as practicable ... but in no event later than sixty (60) days after the expiration'. 'As soon as practicable' is a classic vague standard and the interaction of the two reporting limits is exactly the sort of thing coverage litigation turns on.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its 'first made' requirement must be read with V.A's deeming rule (related claims deemed first made on the earliest date under this or any prior policy) and VI.A's awareness deeming, and with VI.C's separate 60-day clock running from when the Claim is made rather than from policy expiration. In a dispute over which of two consecutive policy years responds, the fit between this grant and those deeming clauses is precisely what a court would have to resolve.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The spousal extension is carefully bounded by two enumerated triggers, an express carve-out for the spouse's own wrongful acts, and a definition of 'spouse' extending to domestic partners. The drafting is tight and self-limiting.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits comfortably with the definitions of Insured Individual and Loss, and nothing elsewhere grants or withdraws spousal coverage. No competing provision was found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short extension to estates, heirs, legal representatives and assigns, with an express exclusion for their own wrongful acts. The categories are enumerated and the limit is stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coheres with the Insured Individual definition and with VIII.I (Bankruptcy), which likewise preserves the parties' positions on insolvency. Nothing contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The ERP right is conditioned on the Insurer's non-renewal or the Parent Company's cancellation and limited to Wrongful Acts occurring before the cancellation/nonrenewal date, but the same paragraph says both that ERP claims are covered and that they are 'deemed to have been made during the immediately preceding Policy Period'. The deeming fiction against the express 'first made during the Extended Reporting Period' requirement is the kind of internal wrinkle a party can exploit.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The election notice must be 'given by the Insured' here, while VIII.J (Authorization Clause) makes the Parent Company the agent for all notices 'except the giving of notice to apply for any Extended Reporting Period' — a deliberate but easily mis-stitched carve-out; the trigger conditions also depend on VIII.C's cancellation mechanics. The Limit sentence duplicates V.A without conflicting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition sweeps in 'any other such documents submitted in connection with the underwriting' and public filings with the DOL or EEOC, a catch-all whose reach after the enumerated applications and attachments is genuinely uncertain. Naming a specific term: 'any other such documents' is the open end.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds VIII.B, which makes all such statements 'the basis of this Policy' and incorporates them, while VIII.K declares the Policy the entire agreement between insureds and insurer — an incorporation-versus-integration tension worth noting. That fight would more likely be pitched on VIII.B or VIII.K.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Perquisites, fringe benefits' and 'any other payment to or for the benefit of an employee arising out of the employment relationship' is a broad catch-all, though the express carve-out of salary, wages, commissions and non-deferred cash incentive compensation cuts it down. The residual boundary between a 'benefit' and 'compensation' can still be argued.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Benefits is used in the Loss carve-outs (items 4 and 6) and in Exclusion B.1, whose proviso restores Benefits coverage for wrongful-termination claims even though Loss item 6 excludes severance payments outright — a live interaction. The definition itself is not contradicted, but its downstream use is uneven.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One line covering breach of 'any oral, written or implied employment contract'; the words are broad but each of the three categories is a familiar legal concept. 'Implied' contract is inherently fact-bound rather than textually ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This coverage trigger sits against Exclusion A.4 (liability of others assumed by contract) and, more pointedly, Exclusion B.3, which limits recovery of 'amounts owing under ... any express written employment contract' to Defense Costs — so the policy grants contract-breach coverage with one hand and strips the damages with the other. That grant/exclusion pairing is a recognised source of coverage disputes.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A written demand against any Insured for monetary or non-monetary relief' is the single most litigated phrase in claims-made policies — what counts as a 'demand', and when 'relief' is being demanded rather than merely complained of, is genuinely contestable. The enumeration is also mechanically damaged: the third subparagraph has lost its letter and the fourth is rendered 'dq.', and the EEOC/OFCCP list is followed by the open-ended 'a similar formal proceeding before another federal, state or other governmental agency'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Everything turns on this definition: Section I covers only Claims 'first made' in the period, V.A deems related Claims first made on the earliest date under this or any prior policy, and III.R defines Potential Claim as an allegation that expressly 'does not constitute a Claim' — drawing the Claim/Potential Claim line is where a two-policy dispute lives. Whether an early letter or EEOC charge was a 'Claim' under the prior year's identical wording is exactly the kind of whole-instrument question this definition forces.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Reasonable and necessary legal fees and expenses' is a standard but genuinely open-textured qualifier, and the parenthetical carve-out for wages and overhead is clear. The vagueness is of the routine, quantum-dispute kind rather than a meaning dispute.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interlocks with V.A (Defense Costs erode the Limit), V.C (consent required before incurring Defense Costs despite the Insurer's duty to defend) and Loss carve-out 7 (no pre-Claim investigation costs), all of which are consistent on their face. No contradiction identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Violation of any Federal, State, or local statute, regulation, ordinance or common law concerning discrimination in employment anywhere in the world' pairs a US-flavoured list of sources with a worldwide reach, leaving foreign discrimination law arguably outside the list it purports to cover. That mismatch between the enumerated legal sources and 'anywhere in the world' is a real general-versus-specific problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: VIII.E (Territory) says the Policy applies to Claims made anywhere in the world and Exclusion A.5 repeatedly says 'anywhere in the world' when it wants foreign law included, which sharpens the omission of foreign statutes here. The tension is genuine but modest and readily harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list has lost the numbering on its final item and turns on qualifiers that shift between subparagraphs — 'directed by the Policyholder' in 2, 'directed solely by the Policyholder' in 3, and 'performs work or services solely for or on behalf of the Policyholder' in 5. Whether 'solely' governs and how an independent contractor qualifies are nameable ambiguities.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Employee here includes independent contractors, yet III.J requires a prior written indemnity agreement before a contractor is an Insured Individual, III.V excludes independent-contractor claims from Third Party Claims, and Exclusion A.9 excludes breach of an express contract with an independent contractor — the policy treats contractors inconsistently across four provisions. That cluster is a plausible whole-instrument problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two carefully specified sexual-harassment limbs are followed by the bare catch-all 'illegal work related harassment', whose reach after the specifics is exactly the ejusdem generis question. 'Illegal' and 'work related' are also undefined boundaries.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Harassment feeds III.X (Wrongful Employment Act) and III.M's trigger list, and nothing elsewhere narrows or contradicts it. The catch-all is expansive but not inconsistent with any other clause.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line composite definition; it does no more than aggregate two other defined terms. There is nothing to construe in it standing alone.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends entirely on III.J and III.O, so any dispute would be about those; no provision uses 'Insured' in a way this definition cannot bear. Checked against Section I and IV.A, which use it consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The five limbs are enumerated with express conditions, but limb 2's 'individuals compensated ... through wages, Salary and/or commissions and whose labor or service is directed by the Policyholder' overlaps awkwardly with the parallel limb in the Employee definition. The 'prior to any Claim ... agreed in writing to indemnify' conditions are, however, precise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Compared with III.G (Employee), the two definitions cover largely the same persons on different conditions, and Section I.A grants coverage for Claims by an 'Employee' against an 'Insured' — so an independent contractor can be a claimant-Employee while not being an Insured Individual. That asymmetry is deliberate in EPL forms but is a place where the instrument does not read cleanly as a whole.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any or all Wrongful Acts that have as a common nexus any fact, circumstance, situation, event, transaction, cause or series of causally or logically connected facts' is notoriously elastic — 'logically connected' in particular has no discernible limit and courts have repeatedly found such relatedness language ambiguous. The term is nameable and its boundary is the whole fight.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the engine of V.A's single-Claim deeming rule ('All Claims arising from the same Wrongful Act and/or all Interrelated Wrongful Acts shall be deemed one Claim ... first made on the earlier date') and of Exclusion A.2(b)'s prior-claim bar, so in any dispute over which policy year responds this definition operates directly against Section I's 'first made during the Policy Period' requirement. Applying it to push a claim back into a prior policy year is precisely a relationship-driven construction question.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long definition with nine carve-outs, several of which are open-textured — 'amounts for which the Insureds are legally or financially absolved from payment', 'matters uninsurable under the law applicable to this Policy' — and the list numbering is corrupted (the ninth item is rendered '2.'). The choice-of-law mechanism for punitive damages is elaborate but self-contained.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Carve-out 2 excludes 'fines or penalties imposed by law' while the closing paragraph and III.S bring in Punitive Damages including ADEA/EPA/FMLA liquidated damages, so a liquidated-damages award can be characterised either way; carve-outs 4 and 6 also sit against Exclusion B.1's write-back of Benefits for wrongful-termination claims. Those are identifiable frictions with III.S and IV.B.1.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The enumeration is mechanically broken — two items numbered '4', a jump to '8', and a page-break heading dropped into the middle — and includes vague entries such as 'failure to grant or adopt adequate employment related policies and procedures'. 'Adequate' is a nameable vague term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The closing limiter ('but only when alleged as part of a Claim for an actual or alleged Breach of Employment Contract, Discrimination, Harassment, Retaliation, or Wrongful Job Action') makes this category wholly parasitic, and III.X lists Other Workplace Torts as an independent limb of Wrongful Employment Act — a mild circularity. Exclusion A.8 also bars emotional-distress claims subject to a proviso that largely undoes it here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure pointer to Item 1 of the Declarations, which names FINRA. There is nothing construable in it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 1 exists and is unambiguous; III.O builds on it consistently. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The Parent Company and its Subsidiaries', with a debtor-in-possession gloss; both components are separately defined and the sentence is definite. The foreign 'similar legal status' phrase is broad but marginal.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on III.U (Subsidiary) and interacts with VIII.A.1 and A.3, which govern when entities join and leave the Policyholder group; those provisions supply the timing rules and do not contradict this one. Checked against VIII.I (Bankruptcy), which is consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short pointer to Item 2, subject to prior termination — the only oddity is the cross-reference, rendered 'Section VLC', pointing to a section that does not exist in that form. A misdirected cross-reference is a mechanical defect, though an obvious one to repair.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Cancellation is actually governed by VIII.C, not VI.C (which is the Awareness Provision's notice clause), so the cross-reference lands on the wrong section as written. The correction is obvious enough that a court would likely fix it rather than construe it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition is deliberately sprawling — 'any substance ... exhibiting any hazardous characteristics', extended to 'noise', 'odor' and 'electric, magnetic or electromagnetic field' — and the 'without limitation' list makes its outer edge indefinite. Pollution definitions of this shape are frequently attacked as overbroad and ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used only in Exclusion A.7, which itself carries a write-back for Employee retaliation claims, and nothing else in this employment-practices form deploys it. Its practical footprint here is small.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'An allegation or accusation ... provided such allegation does not constitute a Claim, but subsequently may give rise to a Claim' is defined negatively against Claim and by a speculative 'may give rise' test, so its boundary is genuinely hard to apply. The line between an accusation and a 'written demand ... for monetary or non-monetary relief' is the ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is defined by exclusion from III.D (Claim) and operates through VI.A, which converts a noticed Potential Claim into a Claim made in the earlier period — so in a dispute about which policy year responds, whether something was a Potential Claim or already a Claim is the pivotal question. That relationship to III.D and VI.A is where the difficulty lies.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A definite definition that names three specific statutes whose liquidated damages are deemed punitive. There is no vague term to seize on.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cuts against Loss carve-out 2 ('fines or penalties imposed by law') and against Exclusion A.5(c)'s express preservation of Equal Pay Act claims, so a statutory liquidated-damages award could be routed through more than one provision. Item 6 of the Declarations elects punitive coverage, which resolves most of it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The illegal retaliatory treatment of Employees, including any retaliatory treatment against an Employee for ...' uses 'including' before four enumerated activities, leaving the general term to do work beyond the list. 'Illegal retaliatory treatment' is broad but has settled legal content.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Retaliation is the carve-out from Exclusions A.5 and A.7, so how far it reaches determines how much of those otherwise sweeping exclusions survives — a genuine interlock worth checking. The provisions are consistent in direction, however.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two numerical control tests stated with precision, plus a timing rule tied to the effective date. The cross-reference is garbled in the scan but the tests themselves are definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It points to Section VIII.A.1 for post-inception entities, and VIII.A.1's 10%/110% employee thresholds are themselves awkward, so the definition inherits whatever difficulty sits there. VIII.A.3 supplies the exit rule consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any natural person who is, or attempted to be, a customer or vendor' is odd and imprecise — what an attempted customer is, and how far 'vendor' reaches, are nameable uncertainties. The independent-contractor carve-out is by contrast clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Third Party Claims are excluded from persons who are independent contractors, yet III.G makes independent contractors 'Employees' whose claims are covered under Insuring Agreement A, and VIII.D makes this Policy excess only as to Third Party Claim losses — the category's boundaries do real work across three provisions. Coverage also depends on Item 7 of the Declarations, which is elected.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line composite pointing to two other defined terms; there is no independent wording to construe. Its content is entirely borrowed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on III.X and III.Z, and Section I uses 'Wrongful Act' consistently with this aggregation. Any fight would be about the component definitions, not this one.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition is a list of six defined categories attributed to three classes of actor, and the third — 'any other persons for whom the Insureds are legally responsible' — is an open-ended catch-all whose reach after the enumerated Policyholder and Insured Individuals is uncertain. The plural 'Other Workplace Torts' also does not match the singular defined term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the trigger for Insuring Agreement A and depends on III.C, III.F, III.H, III.M, III.T and III.Y, each of which has its own soft edge; III.M in turn is defined as covered 'only when alleged as part of a Claim for' the other categories, producing a mild circularity. No direct contradiction was found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The lead-in 'wrongful:' is then repeated inside items 2, 3 and 4, and item 4's 'adverse change in the terms, conditions or status of employment' and item 3's 'deprivation of a career opportunity' are broad and boundary-less. 'Deprivation of a career opportunity' is a nameable vague term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds III.X and works with Exclusion B.1's wrongful-termination write-back, which uses the different phrase 'wrongful termination of employment' rather than the defined Wrongful Job Action — a small drafting mismatch. Otherwise it reads consistently with the rest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The enumerated protected bases are closed with 'or on any other basis prohibited by law', a general catch-all sitting against a long list of specifics — the classic ejusdem generis setup. The opening list of conduct ('error, misstatement, misleading Statement, act, omission, neglect, or breach of duty') is similarly broad before being narrowed by the discrimination requirement.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It only bites if Item 7 elects Third Party Claim coverage, and it works with III.V, which itself excludes independent contractors; the two read together coherently. No contradicting provision was located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is a dense block of twelve exclusions built on repeated open-ended connectors ('in any way involving'), a statutory list in A.5 closed by 'including any other federal, state local or foreign statute or law similar to any statute or law described in (a) through (h)' — an express ejusdem generis clause — and A.12's conduct bar triggered 'if evidenced by any judgment, final adjudication, alternate dispute resolution proceeding or a document or written statement by an Insured'. Each of those is a nameable, frequently litigated ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: A.8 excludes emotional distress but its proviso restores it 'with respect to any actual or alleged mental anguish or emotional distress in a Claim or Third Party Claim for a Wrongful Act by an Insured', which in an employment-practices policy swallows the exclusion almost whole; A.2's prior-and-pending bar also runs on III.K's elastic Interrelated Wrongful Acts and against Section I's grant. Those are specific whole-instrument frictions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The lead-in inverts the usual form ('the Insurer shall only pay Defense Costs, and not other components of Loss'), and item 4 sweeps in 'any request order ... or agreement for non-monetary relief including injunctive relief, declaratory relief, restitution, or any other equitable remedy' with a missing conjunction and an open catch-all. 'Any other equitable remedy' and the garbled 'request order' are both construable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 4 strips damages coverage for non-monetary relief while III.D expressly defines a Claim to include 'a written demand ... for monetary or non-monetary relief' and Section I grants coverage for such Claims; item 1's Benefits write-back for wrongful termination also cuts against Loss carve-outs 4 and 6, which exclude future benefits and severance outright. Those are named, reciprocal tensions with III.D, Section I and III.L.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The limit language itself is precise, but the final paragraph contains a deeming rule of real bite: related Claims are 'deemed one Claim ... first made on the earlier date' either a Claim was first made 'under this Policy or any prior policy' or valid notice was given under any prior policy. Reading that against the closing sentence, which restricts coverage to Claims 'deemed to have been first made during the Policy Period', creates a genuinely contestable relation-back mechanism.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This clause can push a Claim presented during this policy year back into the prior year, directly qualifying Section I's grant, Exclusion A.2's prior-claim bar and VI.A's awareness deeming — and where the file is expressly the '2011/2012 policy', which of two consecutive years responds is the natural battleground. It also has to be squared with II.C's separate ERP deeming rule.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two lines fixing the retention as an excess point borne by the insureds; the amount is in Item 4 and the mechanism is arithmetic. Nothing here is open-textured.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with V.C's 50%-of-retention consent threshold and V.A's erosion of the limit by Defense Costs, both of which use the retention consistently. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause combines a duty to defend with a consent requirement 'which shall not be unreasonably withheld' and a hammer clause keyed to insureds who 'unreasonably refuse to consent' — 'unreasonably' twice, in both directions, is a nameable standard-based ambiguity. It also permits the insurer to stop defending 'after the rejection of a settlement offer as described below', which is loosely tied to the later hammer paragraph.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The bar on insureds incurring Defense Costs without consent sits against the Insurer's own duty to defend and against Loss carve-out 7 (no coverage for costs before something is a Claim), and the hammer clause's 'plus an additional fifty (50) percent' must be reconciled with V.A's absolute aggregate limit — the clause itself supplies that reconciliation. The interlock is dense but broadly coherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The deeming rule refers to 'the Policy Period in which the Potential Claim was first reported', which presupposes a multi-year continuum the single-year Policy Period definition does not supply, and the closing sentence bars coverage for fees incurred 'prior to the time such circumstances result in a Claim'. The awareness trigger — 'becomes aware of a Potential Claim' — is itself a soft threshold.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works directly against III.R (Potential Claim is defined as something that is not a Claim), III.D and Section I's 'first made during the Policy Period' requirement, and it overlaps with V.A's separate relation-back rule; two different deeming mechanisms can point to different periods. In a dispute over which policy year answers, that overlap is exactly what has to be resolved.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A condition precedent with a specific checklist of what a Potential Claim notice must contain, plus a duty to give such further information 'as it may reasonably require'. The list is closed and detailed; only 'reasonably require' is open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supports VI.A and is reinforced by VIII.H, which bars any action against the Insurer absent 'full compliance with all the terms' — so a defective notice has severe consequences, but the provisions point the same way. No inconsistency identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single sentence combining 'as soon as practicable' with a hard 60-day outer limit; 'as soon as practicable' is a familiar vague standard but the backstop makes the operative rule definite. Little else is construable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its 60-day clock runs from when the Claim is first made, while Section I's 60-day clock runs from expiration of the Policy Period, so two different deadlines can apply to the same Claim depending on whether it arose from a noticed Potential Claim. That divergence between VI.C and Section I is a specific, nameable friction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The deeming sentence is internally odd: notices are effective 'upon actual receipt thereof by the addressee or one day following the date such notices are sent, whichever is earlier', so a notice can be deemed received before it actually is. The cross-reference to 'Item 711' is also a mechanical slip for Item 11.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with Item 11's split addresses for claim notices versus all other notices and with VIII.J's authorization of the Parent Company, which excepts ERP election notices; those provisions fit together. The effectiveness rule is the only awkward piece and nothing elsewhere contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The thresholds do not track cleanly: subsection (a) makes a new entity a Subsidiary 'only if' its employees do not exceed ten percent of existing Employees, and the following paragraph gives ninety days' cover where the post-Transaction headcount 'exceeds a hundred and ten percent', with the garbled phrase 'shall provide insurance for such entities ... as for a period of ninety (90) days'. The gap between the two tests and the stray 'as' are both nameable defects.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It amends III.U (Subsidiary), which cross-refers back to this subsection, and its automatic-acquisition rules must be read with VIII.A.2's change-of-control provision and VIII.A.3's cessation rule; the sequence is workable but the thresholds do not mesh precisely with the definition they modify. That is a genuine, if technical, whole-instrument wrinkle.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The runoff mechanism is stated clearly with two enumerated triggers and an express carve-out for receivers and debtor-in-possession status. 'All or substantially all of its assets' is standard but has settled meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says coverage 'shall not be cancellable by the Parent Company', which squarely qualifies VIII.C.1's unconditional right of the Parent Company to cancel during the Policy Period — a specific, named tension, though the more specific clause plainly governs. It also interacts with II.C's ERP trigger, which depends on cancellation by the Parent Company.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two lines with a clear temporal cut-off tied to the date the entity ceased to be a Subsidiary. Nothing open-textured.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says coverage continues 'until termination of the Policy' whereas VIII.A.2 uses 'until termination of the Policy Period' — a slight verbal drift, but no substantive conflict with III.U or VIII.A.1. Consistent with the rest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The severability mechanics are stated with precision — a closed list of officers whose knowledge is imputed to the Policyholder and a bar on imputation between Insured Individuals — though the closing sentence has run together with the preceding numbered item in the scan. The enumerated officer list is the kind of specific that invites an expressio unius argument about anyone omitted.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It incorporates the Application into the Policy and makes those statements 'the basis of this Policy', which sits against VIII.K's declaration that 'this Policy constitutes the entire agreement'; it also parallels Exclusion A.12's separate non-imputation rule for Insured Individuals. That incorporation-versus-integration point is a specific, nameable tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Six numbered rules with definite notice periods, a short-rate refund mechanism and an override for controlling law; the numbering is damaged in the scan but the substance is precise. Nothing genuinely open-textured.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sub-clause 1 gives the Parent Company an unqualified cancellation right that VIII.A.2 expressly negates after a change of control, and cancellation or non-renewal is the gateway condition for the ERP in II.C — so this clause is load-bearing across the instrument. Those relationships are identifiable but reconcilable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The excess-only rule is expressly confined to 'Loss arising from any Third Party Claim', and the closing line — 'in all other events, this Policy is intended to provide primary insurance' — uses the weak 'is intended to' rather than an operative 'is'. That phrasing is a nameable soft spot in an otherwise tight clause.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on III.V (Third Party Claim) and on Item 7's election of that coverage, and it does not conflict with V.B's retention or V.A's limit. Read whole, the split between excess and primary is coherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single sentence granting worldwide territorial scope; short and unqualified, which is the same shape as high-risk short provisions but here has only one plausible meaning. Nothing to name.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reaches Claims made anywhere, while III.F (Discrimination) defines the covered wrong by reference only to 'Federal, State, or local' law and Exclusion A.5 expressly reaches foreign statutes — so worldwide territory does not map perfectly onto the worldwide substance. That is the one identifiable friction, and it is modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conversion mechanism tied to a named published rate and specified conversion dates; the operation is arithmetic. No vague term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It uses the defined terms Retentions and Loss consistently with V.A and V.B and nothing elsewhere addresses currency. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard subrogation, with a broad cooperation duty ('shall do everything necessary'). That phrase is expansive but its content is supplied by the stated purpose of securing recovery rights.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with V.C's cooperation duty and VIII.H's compliance condition precedent without contradiction. Nothing else touches recovery rights.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Full compliance with all the terms of this Policy' as a condition precedent is a sweeping, unqualified requirement that courts often have to soften or read down. The generality of 'all the terms' is the nameable point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It amplifies the specific conditions precedent in Section I (reporting) and VI.B (Potential Claim notice), and any argument about prejudice or substantial compliance would be run against those clauses together. No contradiction, but it makes every other term potentially forfeiting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence preserving the insurer's obligations and defences on insolvency; it is symmetrical and definite. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits III.O's debtor-in-possession language and VIII.A.2's carve-out for receivers and DIP status, and II.B extends coverage to representatives of insolvent Insured Individuals. All point the same way.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The agency grant is broad but its scope is enumerated (notices, premiums, return premiums, endorsements) with one express exception for ERP election notices. The list is closed and the exception is clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It squares with VII ('Notice to the Insureds shall be given to the Parent Company') and with II.C, which requires the ERP election notice to be 'given by the Insured' — the carve-out is what makes those two consistent. Checked and coherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three distinct rules are packed into one paragraph — a written-endorsement requirement, an integration clause, and a no-waiver/no-estoppel rule that runs against both parties — and the anti-waiver sentence is oddly framed as knowledge not effecting a waiver by anyone. The integration statement's reach ('the entire agreement') is the term to name.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The integration clause sits directly against VIII.B, which incorporates the Application and makes its statements 'the basis of this Policy and ... part of this Policy', and against the Declarations' listed endorsements; whether the Application is inside or outside the 'entire agreement' is a specific, identifiable question. That is the clearest Category 2 point in the general conditions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A boilerplate headings clause; its only oddity is that it disclaims headings as part of 'the terms and conditions of coverage' rather than of the Policy generally. That narrowing is unlikely to matter.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The instrument relies heavily on captions and cross-references by section letter (III.D, VIII.C and so on), so a strict reading of this clause is in mild tension with the way the policy navigates itself. The tension is theoretical rather than operative.
